item.scenario: A researcher provides Claude with a technical paper and asks it to quote a specific methodology statement, but doesn't attach the paper. Claude returns a quote in quotation marks that sounds authoritative. Before using this quote in a presentation, what is the most appropriate step?
item.a: Use it as-is, since Claude produced it fluently and with confidence.
item.b: Paraphrase the quote so it's not word-for-word, to avoid accuracy issues.
item.c: Ask Claude whether the quote is accurate before proceeding.
item.d: Find the exact quote word for word in the actual paper to verify it.
item.why: Fabricated quotes need direct verification against the source; confidence and clarity are not evidence, only source material is.
item.quote: Claude can display quotes that may look authoritative or sound convincing, but are not grounded in fact.

item.scenario: A sales manager asks Claude to write a proposal for a new client, requesting specific sections: executive summary, pricing details, implementation timeline, and risk mitigation. Claude produces a polished three-page document with clear headings and professional formatting. The manager checks every number against the client's requirements and finds them all correct. What should the manager do next before sending the proposal?
item.a: Send it immediately, since all the numbers have been verified against the source material.
item.b: Check whether each of the four requested sections is actually present and complete in the proposal.
item.c: Ask Claude to regenerate the proposal to increase confidence in its accuracy.
item.d: Have Claude add more detail to every section to ensure nothing was missed.
item.why: Accuracy checks facts against the source; completeness checks whether the brief's requirements are all there, and these are different checks with different references.
item.quote: A wrong number is on the page, so at least you can see it. A missing point isn't on the page at all, so nothing looks wrong.

item.scenario: A team is building a quarterly budget tracker that they'll refine and reuse every three months, with the same client files and formatting rules applied each time. Where should they set this up in Claude?
item.a: In plain chat, creating the tracker from scratch each quarter.
item.b: Using Research to find external benchmarking data for budgets.
item.c: In a Project, where the knowledge and instructions are saved and ready every time.
item.d: As a live artifact in Claude Cowork to hand off the work to others.
item.why: A Project is the right feature for work that comes back repeatedly with the same files and rules, providing a persistent workspace that doesn't require setting it up from scratch each time.
item.quote: Will this work come back, with the same files and rules? Do it in a Project: a workspace with its own knowledge and instructions, ready every time.
